ela_passages.title: Martial Arts for the Mind and Body

sentence_paragraphs.text: The martial arts blend a series of physical movements with strategic mental discipline so that practitioners can defend themselves, physically defeat an opponent, or both.
Historians are unsure of exactly when and where martial arts were first used.
Martial arts have been practiced by several different societies for many centuries.
Martial arts such as karate, kung fu, tae kwon do, and judo are still taught and practiced as methods of self-defense, but they offer students more than that.
The study of martial arts can provide students with a way to enhance their mental discipline as well as their physical fitness.
Discipline, focus, and respect are important qualities for everyone to have.
However, for most people these qualities are not innate; they must be learned and practiced.
The study of martial arts can provide an opportunity to develop these skills.
Students are rewarded for their dedication by passing tests and advancing to higher ranks or levels.

For example, in a typical tae kwon do class, students learn discipline by diligently practicing moves, improve focus by listening carefully, and demonstrate respect by bowing to the instructor and following directions.
For teenagers, martial arts classes provide a safe and structured environment for gaining physical skills, building confidence, and enjoying a sense of community.
A lot of teens go through hard situations as they try to do well in school and in life.
A martial arts class can provide teens with a physical outlet for stress while also challenging them mentally.
Participating in a martial arts program also helps children and teens focus on self-improvement rather than on competition.
Progressing through levels of achievement involves mastering more physically demanding techniques.
It requires students to take responsibility and be accountable for achieving set goals.
Students gain confidence and experience companionship with other students who are progressing through the ranks.
Adults who practice martial arts can experience many of the same benefits that younger people do, but perhaps the greatest of these is health and fitness.
Adult martial arts students often see changes in their body within weeks of beginning a program.
For people interested in studying a martial art, there are many ways to learn and practice.
In addition to private studios, community recreation centers often offer low-cost or free martial arts classes.
There are even online videos that introduce students to the basic concepts.
People should study martial arts.

questions.question: What is the best way to combine sentences 2 and 3?

options.A: Historians, who are unsure of exactly when and where martial arts were first used, know that martial arts have been practiced by several different societies for many centuries.
options.B: While historians are unsure of exactly when and where martial arts were first used, they do know that martial arts have been practiced by several different societies for many centuries.
options.C: Because historians know that martial arts have been practiced by several different societies for many centuries, they are unsure of exactly when and where martial arts were first used.
options.D: Martial arts have been practiced by several different societies for many centuries, and historians are unsure of exactly when and where martial arts were first used.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the best way to combine sentences 2 and 3.

A. Incorrect. This way of combining sentences 2 and 3 places unnecessary emphasis on characterizing historians, and it does not clearly show the contrasting relationship between the idea from sentence 2 that historians do not know the exact origins of martial arts and the idea in sentence 3 that historians know that martial arts have a long history.

B. CORRECT. This option is correct because the word “while” at the beginning of the sentence best indicates the contrast between the ideas in sentences 2 and 3. Sentence 2 states that historians do not know the exact origins of martial arts (“unsure of exactly when and where”). Sentence 3 describes what historians do know about these origins (“practiced by several different societies for many centuries”). This combination indicates that historians have a general understanding about the origins of martial arts even though they cannot confirm the exact details.

C. Incorrect. Starting this sentence with the word “because” indicates a cause-and-effect relationship that does not exist between the ideas in the original sentences. The idea from sentence 3, that historians know that martial arts have been practiced for many years, did not cause the idea in sentence 2, that historians do not know exact details about the origins of martial arts.

D. Incorrect. The conjunction (connecting word) “and” does not clearly show how the ideas in sentences 2 and 3 are related. While “and” can be used to combine related sentences, it does not demonstrate the contrast between the idea in sentence 2, that historians do not know the exact origins of martial arts, and the idea in sentence 3, that historians know that martial arts have a long history.

questions.question: Where should sentence 10 be moved to improve the organization of the second paragraph (sentences 6–10)?

options.A: to the beginning of the paragraph (before sentence 6)
options.B: between sentences 6 and 7
options.D: between sentences 8 and 9

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks where sentence 10 should be moved to improve the organization of the second paragraph.

A. Incorrect. Starting this paragraph with sentence 10 would weaken the paragraph's organization because it would place a supporting detail sentence (sentence 10) before the topic sentence (sentence 6). Sentence 6 belongs at the beginning of the paragraph because it introduces the topic—the qualities of discipline, focus, and respect. Sentence 10 supports the key idea of the paragraph, that these qualities can be developed through the study of martial arts. If sentence 10 preceded sentence 6, the transitional phrase “for example” would refer to an unspecified topic and idea.

B. Incorrect. Sentence 6 presents the idea that “discipline, focus, and respect are important qualities for everyone to have,” but the example in sentence 10 does not directly relate to this idea. Sentence 10 explains how martial arts develop these qualities, not why they are important qualities to have. Because sentence 10 is not directly related to the idea in sentence 6 (the qualities are important), it should not follow sentence 6.

C. Incorrect. Sentences 7 and 8 should not be separated, because the idea presented in sentence 8—that “the study of martial arts can provide an opportunity to develop these skills”—is directly related to the idea from sentence 7—that the skills of discipline, focus, and respect “are not innate; they must be learned and practiced.” Sentence 10 supports the idea from sentence 8 by describing an example from a typical martial arts class, so sentence 10 should not precede sentence 8.

D. CORRECT. This option is correct because sentence 10 logically follows and supports the idea in sentence 8 that “the study of martial arts can provide an opportunity to develop” the qualities of discipline, focus, and respect. Sentence 10 explains this idea with examples, describing three specific ways that students in a typical tae kwon do class develop discipline, focus, and respect—by “diligently practicing,” “listening carefully,” and “bowing to the instructor and following directions.”

questions.question: Which revision of sentence 12 best maintains the formal style established in the passage?

options.A: A lot of teens have to put up with difficult things while trying to do well in school and in life.
options.B: Many teenagers deal with tough situations as they try to stay on top of their studies and do well in life.
options.C: Many teenagers encounter challenges as they work to succeed both academically and personally.
options.D: A lot of teens face problems as they work to keep up with their schoolwork and find personal success.

C. CORRECT. This option is correct because it uses clear and scholarly wording throughout the whole sentence. The phrases “many teenagers,” “encounter challenges,” and “succeed both academically and personally” make the sentence's style more consistently formal than the other options.

D. Incorrect. The phrases “A lot,” “face problems,” and “keep up with” are worded informally; therefore, this sentence does not consistently maintain the formal style established in the passage.

questions.question: Which transitional phrase should be added to the beginning of sentence 17?

options.A: Over time,
options.B: In fact,
options.D: For instance,

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the transitional phrase that should be added to the beginning of sentence 17.

A. CORRECT. This option is correct because it best shows the chronological progression between the idea in sentence 16—progressing through levels of achievement “requires students to take responsibility and be accountable for achieving set goals”—and the idea in sentence 17—“students gain confidence and experience companionship with other students who are progressing through the ranks.” The transitional phrase “over time” shows the gradual nature of the relationship between the cause in sentence 16 and the effect in sentence 17.

B. Incorrect. The phrase “in fact” is used to emphasize or add support to a preceding statement, but sentence 17 does not simply reinforce the idea in sentence 16; rather, it describes a result that develops gradually over time, which “in fact” does not convey.

C. Incorrect. The phrase “even so” signals a contrast or an unexpected outcome, but there is no contrast between the ideas in sentence 16, that progressing through levels requires responsibility and accountability, and sentence 17, that students gain confidence and companionship; sentence 17 is a natural continuation of sentence 16, not a contrasting idea.

D. Incorrect. The phrase “for instance” introduces a specific example of a preceding general statement, but sentence 17 does not provide a specific example of the idea in sentence 16; instead, it describes an additional, related effect that develops over time.

questions.question: Which sentence would best follow and support sentence 18?

options.A: Adults often enjoy spending time with other students in their martial arts class.
options.B: Adults who study martial arts can apply the discipline they learn to other parts of their lives.
options.C: For example, some adults lose weight and gain muscle tone after only a few months of training.
options.D: In fact, many adults begin studying martial arts because a friend or family member recommended it.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence would best follow and support sentence 18.

B. Incorrect. While this option relates to a benefit adults may experience, it focuses on discipline rather than the health and fitness benefit identified as “the greatest” in sentence 18, so it does not directly support sentence 18.

questions.question: Which sentence should be added after sentence 23 to best conclude the passage?

options.A: Martial arts classes are often more affordable than other extracurricular activities for students.
options.B: Whether people choose a formal class or an online video, martial arts offer benefits to practitioners of any age.
options.C: Many people who begin studying a martial art eventually go on to teach others.
options.D: The specific martial art that a person chooses to study often depends on what is available in their area.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence should be added after sentence 23 to best conclude the passage.

A. Incorrect. The affordability of martial arts classes is not a main idea developed throughout the passage, so this option does not serve as an effective concluding sentence.

B. CORRECT. This option is correct because it ties together the passage's main ideas: the variety of ways to learn (introduced in the final paragraph) and the broad benefits to practitioners of any age (discussed throughout the passage for teens and adults alike), making it an effective concluding statement.

C. Incorrect. The idea that students go on to teach others is not developed anywhere else in the passage, so this option introduces a new idea rather than concluding the passage's established ideas.

D. Incorrect. While sentence 23 mentions ways to learn martial arts, this option shifts focus to availability by location, which is not a theme developed in the passage, so it does not effectively conclude the passage.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Misty Copeland is best known for becoming the first Black female principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre. (2) Copeland is an American dancer and author. (3) Copeland was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People in 2015.

What is the best way to combine these sentences to clarify the relationship between ideas?

options.A: Misty Copeland, best known for becoming the first Black female principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre, is an American dancer and author who was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People in 2015.
options.B: Misty Copeland was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People in 2015, and she is an American dancer and author who is best known for becoming the first Black female principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre.
options.C: Misty Copeland, best known for becoming the first Black female principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre, is an American dancer and author; in addition, she was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People in 2015.
options.D: Misty Copeland, an American dancer and author, was named one of Time's 100 Most Influential People in 2015, and she is best known for becoming the first Black female principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre.

solution.exhibit_text:
(A) introduces Copeland by what she's best known for, then who she is, then builds to the award. (B) and (D) use "and" to place her career and the award at the same level. (C) uses the wordier "in addition, she was" instead of the clearer "who was."

**Why this sounds right:** Lumping her achievements together with "and" still reads as a fluent sentence, so the structural issue of ordering doesn't register as an error.

**The concept:** When combining several short sentences about one subject, there's usually one "main point" and the rest are supporting details. The strongest combination makes the main point the main clause and folds the other facts in as describing phrases or clauses, in whatever order makes the most logical sense. Watch out for answers that just string everything together with "and," since that treats every fact as equally important and loses the sense of what matters most.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- Weak: "The bakery opens at six. It sells fresh croissants. Many customers line up before it opens." Stronger: "Many customers line up before the bakery opens at six to buy its fresh croissants." (Folds the supporting details into one sentence built around the real main point.)
- Weak: "The lake freezes every winter. Skaters flock to it. The ice can get over a foot thick." Stronger: "Every winter, skaters flock to the lake as it freezes to over a foot thick." (Same fix — one main clause, details folded in.)

grammar_questions.question:
(1) The small town of Elmsworth has long been known for its devotion to preserving local history. (2) Recently, local leaders proposed a new initiative to convert the abandoned train depot into a public library and community archive. (3) Filled with vintage rail memorabilia and handwritten letters, the historical society hopes the new archive will inspire local students. (4) If the town council approves the funding next month, construction will likely begin before the arrival of spring.

Which sentence in the paragraph contains an error in construction and should be revised? There is only one error in construction.

options.A: Sentence 1
options.B: Sentence 2
options.D: Sentence 4

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 3, "Filled with vintage rail memorabilia and handwritten letters" is placed right next to "the historical society," which illogically suggests the society itself is filled with memorabilia. The modifier needs to describe the archive, not the historical society.

**Why this sounds right:** "The historical society" is a plausible, active-sounding subject that fits the sentence's larger point about hopes for the archive, so it's easy to miss that an organization can't literally be "filled with" memorabilia — that's the archive.

**The concept:** When a sentence opens with a describing phrase followed by a comma, whatever noun comes right after that comma is what the phrase is describing. If that noun can't logically do or experience what the phrase describes, the modifier is "dangling" — it has nothing correct to attach to. Fix it by moving the right noun right after the comma, or by rewriting the phrase so it fits the noun that's actually there.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- "After practicing for months, the piano recital finally arrived." (The recital didn't practice — should be "After practicing for months, Mia finally performed in the piano recital.")
- "Having forgotten her umbrella, the rain soaked through her jacket." (The rain didn't forget anything — should be "Having forgotten her umbrella, Priya got soaked in the rain.")

grammar_questions.question:
Priya browsed the antique shop looking for some neat items for her study. After searching through a crate of old postcards, she finally discovered a brass magnifying glass that possessed exactly the vintage charm she had imagined. With a leather-bound atlas tucked under her arm alongside it, she headed home, satisfied that she had found the perfect additions to her study without exceeding her budget.

What is the most precise revision for the words *some neat items for her study*?

options.A: some interesting items for her study
options.B: a vintage magnifying glass and atlas
options.D: two kinds of antique furniture

solution.exhibit_text:
(B) gives the most precise description of what Priya was shopping for — the exact items described in the rest of the paragraph. The other choices use the vague "interesting items" and "old-fashioned things," or name the wrong category of object ("furniture").

**Why this sounds right:** "Some neat items for her study" is a completely natural, casual way to talk — it isn't objectively broken, just vaguer than the specific items the paragraph already names.

**The concept:** Precise language replaces vague, generic words ("things," "a big distance," "what was happening") with specific, concrete details — exact names, numbers, or nouns — that tell the reader precisely what's being described. When comparing answer choices, prefer the one with the most specific, checkable information instead of just restating the same vagueness in fancier words.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- "The volunteers did a bunch of stuff to help clean up the park." → "The volunteers planted new trees and collected forty bags of trash to clean up the park." ("A bunch of stuff" tells the reader nothing concrete.)
- "The scientist made a big discovery about the ocean." → "The scientist discovered a new species of deep-sea jellyfish." ("A big discovery" is vague; name the actual discovery.)

To make it more precise, the answer choice should give more specific information about the "things." (D) gives the most precise description of what Lucia was looking for: affordable salad bowls and serving spoons. grammar_questions.question:
(1) Both Japanese origami and Chinese paper-cutting are traditional paper crafts, but they differ in technique, tools, and purpose. (2) Origami is often practiced by folding a single uncut sheet of paper into intricate three-dimensional shapes without any glue or scissors. (3) The practice of Chinese paper-cutting involves a sharp blade, and scissors, which is used to carve detailed designs into folded red paper. (4) Origami traditionally uses plain or patterned squares; paper-cutting, however, often uses red paper, which symbolizes good fortune and is tinted for festive occasions.

Which pair of revisions need to be made in this paragraph?

options.A: Sentence 1: Delete the comma after crafts AND change they differ to it differs.
options.B: Sentence 2: Change folding to folds AND change shapes to shape.
options.C: Sentence 3: Delete the comma after blade AND change is to are.
options.D: Sentence 4: Delete the semicolon after squares AND change symbolizes to symbolize.

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 3, the comma after "blade" wrongly separates the two tools ("a sharp blade and scissors"), and "is" should be the plural "are" to match that two-item subject.

**Why this sounds right:** The comma after "blade" reads like a natural pause before one more detail, so it doesn't register as splitting a two-item list; and with "scissors" sitting closest to "is," the verb still feels locally fine even though it doesn't match the full two-part subject.

**The concept:** A comma goes before "and" when it separates the last item in a list of three or more, or when "and" is joining two complete, independent sentences. But when "and" is just linking two verbs or phrases that share the same subject, no comma belongs before it — adding one wrongly suggests a third list item, or a second full sentence, that isn't actually there.

**The concept:** Subject-verb agreement means the verb has to match whether its subject is singular or plural ("the museum becomes," not "the museum become"). Pronoun agreement works the same way — a pronoun has to match the number of the noun it refers back to. These two rules often get tested together in the same sentence, so check both the verb and any pronouns against their subject/antecedent, not just one or the other.

**More examples of this mistake:**
- "The chef chopped the vegetables, and seasoned the soup." (No comma needed — "and seasoned" shares the same subject, "the chef"; it isn't a second full sentence.)
- "The hikers reached the summit, and admired the view for an hour." (Same fix — delete the comma.)
- "The twins, who share a room, enjoys decorating it with their own posters, and keeps her side spotless." (Two separate agreement slips in one sentence: "enjoys" should be "enjoy" to match "the twins," and "her" should be "their" since both twins are being described.)
- "The scientists, who collaborate closely, publishes its findings together, and shares all the credit." (Same double-slip pattern: "publishes" should be "publish," and "its" should be "their.")

base_question.question: Which pair of revisions need to be made in this paragraph?
base_question.stimulus: (1) Both Salvadoran and Mexican tamales are delicious staples of Mesoamerican cuisine, but they differ in preparation, wrapping, and texture. (2) Salvadoran tamales are often prepared by pre-cooking the masa, a ground corn dough, into a thick, smooth roux before steaming it, resulting in a silky, custard-like texture that is much softer and wetter than that of typical Mexican tamales. (3) The preparation of Mexican tamales involves a fat, and broth, which is mixed into the masa before steaming. (4) Mexican tamales are traditionally wrapped in dried corn husks; Salvadoran tamales, however, are wrapped in banana leaves, which give them an earthy flavor and tint them slightly green.

options.A: Sentence 1: Delete the comma after cuisine AND change they differ to it differs.
options.B: Sentence 2: Delete the comma after dough AND change is to are.
options.C: Sentence 3: Delete the comma after fat AND change is to are.
options.D: Sentence 4: Delete the semicolon after husks AND change tint to tints.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Multiple
Getting to the Answer: The question is directing you to determine which proposed revisions are correct. Briskly work through each sentence to identify if it contains any errors with punctuation, verb agreement, or modifiers. For Sentence 1, the comma after "cuisine" correctly separates the two complete thoughts using the FANBOYS conjunction "but." Additionally, it uses the plural "they differ" to refer to the plural antecedent "tamales." Eliminate (A). For Sentence 2, the comma after "dough" is correct because it offsets the parenthetical information "a ground corn dough." Furthermore, the singular "is" correctly agrees with the singular "texture." Eliminate (B). For Sentence 3, the comma after "fat" is incorrect because it separates the second ingredient ("broth") from the first ("a fat"). Additionally, "is" should be the plural verb "are" to match the two subjects ("a fat and broth"). (C) is the correct revision to make. On test day, select this answer choice and move on. But, for reference, in Sentence 4, the semicolon after "husks" correctly separates two independent clauses, and the plural verb "tint" correctly matches the other plural verb ("give") in the compound predicate "give... and tint..." of the subject "which," which is plural because it refers to the "banana leaves." (D) is incorrect.
